props.title: With Six You Get Eggroll
props.initialSlug: Blended families never felt so fun!

sections.content: With Six You Get Eggroll represents a pivotal moment in Doris Day's filmography, arriving as her final theatrical film before transitioning to television. This romantic comedy about blended families tackled modern relationships years before The Brady Bunch (1969) hit television screens. Day stars as widow Abby McClure running a lumber yard while raising three sons, who falls for Brian Keith's character Jake Iverson, a widower with a teenage daughter. The film captures the cultural shift of the late 1960s, particularly regarding changing family dynamics and women in business, while maintaining the wholesome charm Day was known for in earlier hits like Pillow Talk (1959) and The Thrill of It All (1963).

sections.content: The late 1960s marked a significant transition in how Hollywood portrayed family dynamics. While With Six You Get Eggroll maintained a relatively conservative approach, it helped pave the way for more complex portrayals of blended families in films like The Stepfather (1987) and Stepmom (1998). The film's approach to showing workplace dynamics - with Day's character running a traditionally male-dominated business - was quietly progressive for its era, predating similar themes in Baby Boom (1987) and Working Girl (1988). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Family Comedy

The influence of With Six You Get Eggroll can be traced through decades of family-merger comedies. While modern entries like Cheaper by the Dozen (2003) and Blended (2014) amp up the chaos for bigger laughs, they follow similar emotional beats established by Day's film. The careful balance of romantic comedy with family dynamics created a template that continues in films like The Parent Trap (1998) and Life of the Party (2018).
